conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for making time for this. I’m Dr. Carter, a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the EPDS—short for Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the week since your baby arrived. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an urgent safety concern, and you’re free to pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. We’ll take it one question at a moment, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Ready to begin?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

(soft sigh) Um… not very often. I laughed a little once—my partner made a goofy face while changing her diaper—but even then it felt… distant, like I was watching it happen instead of really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess… most of the time I can’t really laugh at all. Maybe once or twice something felt a tiny bit funny, but it’s like the joy just doesn’t reach me the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with friends, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like one more chore. I do still look forward to my baby’s tiny smiles, but everything else feels pretty flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I’m holding her wrong or I ate something that bothered her. I know it’s probably not my fault, but the guilty thoughts just keep looping.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke, or I’ll lie awake picturing the crib railing snapping. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the crib’s fine—but I can’t turn the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. Once, I was just folding her tiny onesies and suddenly my chest felt tight, like I couldn’t get enough air. Nothing had happened—no loud noise, no bad news—but I had to sit on the floor and hug my knees until the shaking stopped. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me rattled the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks. Yesterday she cried for twenty minutes while I tried to heat a bowl of soup, and I just stood there crying too because I couldn’t do both. I get through it, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—did I burp her long enough, what if her blanket’s too loose, what if I oversleep and she needs me? I finally drift off, then jolt awake at every tiny sound. I’d guess I’m actually sleeping maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that follows me around, even when I’m holding her and she’s calm. I’ll be smiling for her, but inside it’s just this heavy sadness I can’t shake.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was in the shower—just started sobbing because I felt like I’m failing her even though she was fine. The other time was after a phone call with my mom; I hung up and the tears came out of nowhere.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(quiet voice) A couple of times, yeah. Nothing planned—just a flash, like “what if I could disappear for a while.” I’d never leave her, but the thought popped in when I was rocking her at 3 a.m. and felt totally spent. It scared me enough that I put the baby monitor on my nightstand so my partner would hear if something happened.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (EPDS items paraphrased):

1. Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, joy “doesn’t reach me.”  
2. Loss of anticipatory pleasure; only infant’s smiles evoke positive expectation.  
3. Pervasive inappropriate guilt re parenting competence.  
4–5. Daily free-floating anxiety, situational panic (chest tightness, shaking) without objective trigger.  
6. Overwhelmed by routine tasks; describes “drowning” and simultaneous crying with infant.  
7. Mood-related insomnia: initial and maintenance difficulties, ~4 h fragmented sleep/night.  
8–9. Persistent dysphoria, daily “gray cloud,” spontaneous crying episodes (≥2×/week).  
10. Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I could disappear”) without plan or intent; states fear of own thoughts and ensured monitor placement for safety.

Patterns: Consistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety/panic, functional impairment, and sleep disruption. Passive suicidal cognitions reported.

Screening significance:  
– Meets probable criteria for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.  
– Safety concern: presence of self-harm thoughts → warrants immediate risk assessment and safety planning.

Next steps: Provide scoring sheet, arrange formal follow-up (OB, psychiatry, or crisis team) within 24 h; review supports, crisis resources, and infant care options.
